description_full: Pilgrim's Pride Corporation produces, processes, markets, and distributes fresh, frozen, and value-added chicken and pork products to retailers, distributors, and foodservice operators in the United States, Europe, and Mexico. The company offers fresh products, including refrigerated whole or cut-up chicken, selected chicken parts that are either marinated or non-marinated, primary pork cuts, added value pork, pork ribs, and lamb products; and prepared products, which include fully cooked, ready-to-cook and individually frozen chicken parts, strips, nuggets and patties, processed sausages, bacon, smoked meat, gammon joints, pre-packed meats, sandwich and deli counter meats, and meat balls and coated foods. It also provides plant-based protein, ready-to-eat meals, multi-protein frozen food, vegetarian food, and desserts. In addition, its exported products include whole chickens and chicken parts for distributors in the U.S. or frozen for distribution to export markets and primary pork cuts, hog heads, and trotters frozen for distribution. The company offers its products under the Pilgrim's, Just BARE, Gold'n Pump, Gold Kist, County Pride, Pierce Chicken, Pilgrim's Mexico, To-Ricos, Del Dia, Moy Park, Matteson's, Richmond, Fridge Raiders, and Denny brands. It serves chain restaurants, food processors, broad-line distributors, and other institutions; and retail market, such as grocery store chains, wholesale clubs, and other retail distributors. The company was founded in 1946 and is headquartered in Greeley, Colorado. Pilgrim's Pride Corporation operates as a subsidiary of JBS N.V.

financial_summary: Pilgrim's Pride Corporation is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $6.7B market cap on $18.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 20% against a 6% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 10% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $653M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.0×.

Management returns a meaningful 29.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 82% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Gross margin trails most Consumer Defensive peers — competitors appear to have the pricing hand
Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.
